s1.title: How to power up your product by machine learning with python microservice, pt. 1
s1.summary: This is an introductory workshop article from the Europython 2019 series about integrating machine learning into software products, particularly through Python microservices and a microservice-oriented architecture. It discusses organizational readiness, data and infrastructure prerequisites, machine-learning project workflows, data-platform boundaries and SLAs, deployment approaches, and the decision to expose models as batch jobs, reports, or real-time Model-as-a-Service APIs.

s2.title: Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline: How to build scalable Machine Learning systems - Part 2/2
s2.summary: This technical article describes an architecture for a scalable, production-oriented machine-learning pipeline rather than a specific organization’s system. It discusses separating offline model development from online serving; event-driven ingestion, feature storage, training, evaluation, deployment, scoring, and monitoring; and decisions involving scalability, latency, fault tolerance, model versioning, data lineage, testing, and reusable design patterns.

s3.title: Some Thoughts on Modularization in Machine Learning
s3.summary: This is an opinion essay on software architecture for machine-learning-enabled applications, rather than a document about a specific organization or project. It advocates isolating machine-learning functionality behind APIs or microservices, separating data-science and application-development responsibilities, managing implementation complexity, and avoiding conflicts between model-performance and product-engagement metrics.

s4.title: Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture
s4.summary: This presentation by Iguazio describes an architecture for productionizing machine-learning workloads with microservices. It discusses using Kubernetes, Spark, Nuclio, MLRun, and Kubeflow for distributed data preparation, training, deployment, autoscaling, versioning, monitoring, drift detection, and CI/CD, including real-time inference and feedback workflows.

s5.title: Microservices Suck for Machine Learning (and what we did about it)
s5.summary: This article examines machine-learning workflows in microservice-based systems, using Reddit-style services and referencing feature-store implementations at Airbnb, Uber, and Lyft. It discusses feature collection, low-latency serving, and point-in-time-correct training data, and describes event streams, persistent logs, materialized views, and a centralized feature store, including schema, migration, cost, and operational trade-offs.

s6.title: MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning
s6.summary: This Google Cloud architecture document explains MLOps practices for machine-learning systems. It discusses automating CI, CD, and continuous training; integrating data and model validation, metadata, feature stores, monitoring, and pipeline triggers; and progressing from manual workflows to automated ML pipelines and CI/CD for reproducible training, deployment, retraining, and model serving.

s7.title: Composing Deep-Learning Microservices for the Hybrid Internet of Things
s7.summary: This is a technical architecture article about deploying deep-learning applications as microservices across hybrid cloud and Internet of Things environments. It discusses containerization, serverless execution, fog-based distribution to constrained edge devices, middleware for messaging and orchestration, and OpenWhisk-based event-driven service composition and chaining.

s8.title: Continuous Intelligence: Moving Machine Learning Application into Production Reliably
s8.summary: This is a Thoughtworks presentation about Continuous Delivery for Machine Learning (CD4ML) and an example retail demand-prediction system. It discusses design decisions for versioning data, code, models, and experiments; orchestrating training, testing, deployment, and infrastructure across environments; assessing model performance; and monitoring production models and data.

s9.title: Architecture of a real-world Machine Learning system
s9.summary: This article, part of a series on machine-learning platforms supported by Digital Catapult and PAPIs, describes a real-world supervised-learning system with client-server prediction. It discusses component boundaries and workflows for data collection and labeling, featurization, model training and evaluation, orchestration, serving, monitoring, and front-end integration, including model updates, canary testing, A/B testing, and rollback.

s10.title: Architecting a Machine Learning System for Risk
s10.summary: This is an Airbnb engineering document describing the architecture of a machine-learning system for near-real-time online risk and fraud mitigation. It discusses separating feature extraction from scoring, using Java services and Openscoring with PMML, designing an agile model-building and deployment pipeline, and addressing tradeoffs involving latency, robustness, model compatibility, ground-truth quality, and future online learning.

s11.title: Architecting a Scalable Real Time Learning System
s11.summary: This technical architecture article from Fourkind describes a scalable real-time online-learning system, illustrated with an AWS-based recommendation engine. It discusses selecting linear incremental-learning algorithms, streaming and ordering training data, atomic model versioning, separating training from horizontally scalable inference, storing features and state, logging events, and handling throughput-related model lag.

s12.title: System Architectures for Personalization and Recommendation
s12.summary: This technical architecture article describes Netflix’s personalization and recommendation system. It discusses combining offline, nearline, and online computation; managing model training, data and event distribution, signals, and recommendation-result storage; and balancing freshness, latency, scalability, consistency, and experimentation flexibility.

s13.title: Architectural thinking in the Wild West of data science
s13.summary: This article presents architectural guidance for enterprise data-science projects, drawing on IBM’s architecture methods and data-and-analytics reference architecture. It discusses uncontrolled technology choices, poor reproducibility and reuse, limited collaboration, documentation, and insufficient attention to non-functional requirements such as scalability and maintainability. It also considers architect and data-scientist responsibilities, governance, process models, deployment practices, and data-platform components.

s14.title: Machine Learning Architecture: The Core Components
s14.summary: This is an explanatory architecture article about generic machine-learning solutions, rather than a named organization or project. It outlines decisions and responsibilities for data generation and collection, feature engineering, model training and evaluation, task orchestration, prediction, infrastructure, authentication, user interaction, and monitoring, emphasizing that feature engineering should not be omitted.

s15.title: Scalable Software and Big Data Architecture - Big Data and Analytics Architectural Patterns
s15.summary: This is an overview article in a series on scalable software and big-data architecture, published by InnoArchiTech. It discusses architectural patterns and decisions for data storage and modeling, acquisition and integration, availability and scalability, processing and movement, and data access, analytics, and business intelligence.

s16.title: Machine Learning in Production: Software Architecture
s16.summary: This is an excerpted software-architecture chapter from *Machine Learning in Production*, presented by Domino for data scientists integrating models into existing systems. It discusses selecting and combining client-server, n-tier/service-oriented, microservice, and monolithic architectures, including tradeoffs involving latency, infrastructure and development costs, modularity, code reuse, maintainability, and cognitive overhead.

s17.title: AutoML
s17.summary: This IBM informational document concerns AutoML, including IBM Watson Studio AutoAI and the Lale library. It discusses automating feature engineering, hyperparameter optimization, neural architecture search, and model selection, along with workflow integration, explainability, environmental costs, and the roles of data scientists and analysts.

s18.title: AutoML is Overhyped
s18.summary: This is an opinion article about automated machine-learning tools and their use in organizational data-science projects. It describes AutoML decisions across preprocessing, feature engineering, feature selection, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and ensembling, and discusses whether boxed tools save time, address staffing gaps, or outperform manually developed models.

s19.title: Three Levels of ML Software
s19.summary: This technical architecture guide concerns machine-learning software projects and MLOps practices, organizing work around data, models, and code. It discusses data and model engineering pipelines, offline versus online training and prediction patterns, model serialization formats, serving arrangements, monitoring, retraining, and deployment using containers or serverless functions.

s20.title: MLOps: Methods and Tools of DevOps for Machine Learning
s20.summary: This article is a technical overview of MLOps, an operational framework for managing machine-learning systems from training through production and retraining. It discusses decisions around data and model versioning, validation, continuous integration and delivery, continuous training, model serving, monitoring for drift, workflow orchestration, deployment patterns, tool selection, and levels of automation.

s21.title: MLOps: What It Is, Why it Matters, and How To Implement It (from a Data Scientist Perspective)
s21.summary: This is a practitioner-oriented technical article about MLOps for machine-learning teams and production systems, drawing partly on an in-house pipeline effort in Mozambique. It discusses lifecycle architecture decisions including experiment and artifact tracking, automated training/deployment, testing, monitoring for drift and training-serving skew, maturity levels, and build-versus-buy or hybrid infrastructure choices.

s22.title: MLOps Principles
s22.summary: This is a principles and best-practices document from SIG MLOps concerning the development and operation of machine-learning software systems. It discusses lifecycle phases, automation and CI/CD, continuous training and monitoring, versioning and experiment tracking, testing, reproducibility, modular architecture, deployment, and metrics for ML delivery and production readiness.

s23.title: Machine Learning Monitoring: What It Is, and What We Are Missing
s23.summary: This is a blog article from Evidently AI about monitoring production machine-learning systems. It discusses extending observability beyond software health metrics to include data quality, drift, model performance, fairness, business outcomes, and silent failures, while addressing monitoring ownership, cross-team collaboration, alerting, retraining, and integration with the MLOps lifecycle.

s24.title: Automated monitoring of your machine learning models with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor and sending predictions to human review workflows using Amazon A2I
s24.summary: This AWS Machine Learning Blog post describes a sample Amazon SageMaker workflow for breast-cancer classification using XGBoost, Model Monitor, and Amazon Augmented AI (A2I). It discusses capturing inference data, establishing monitoring baselines and schedules, detecting data-quality or drift violations, and routing low-confidence predictions to human reviewers for correction and possible retraining.

s25.title: MLOps: Model management, deployment, and monitoring with Azure Machine Learning
s25.summary: This Azure documentation article describes MLOps capabilities and workflows for the Azure Machine Learning platform. It discusses decisions for reproducible pipelines and environments, model registration and packaging, deployment to cloud, edge, or local targets, governance and lineage, monitoring and drift detection, controlled rollouts, retraining, and CI/CD automation.

s26.title: The Pros and Cons of Using Jupyter Notebooks as Your Editor for Data Science Work TL;DR: PyCharm's probably better
s26.summary: This article examines the use of Jupyter Notebooks as editors in data-science and machine-learning workflows, comparing them with Spyder and PyCharm. It discusses prototyping, secure server-side execution, collaboration, versioning, credential and transformation duplication, plot distribution, and production deployment. It proposes using an IDE and maintaining each transformation in one reusable, productionized repository location, while retaining notebooks for suitable exploratory tasks.

s27.title: 10 reasons why data scientists love Jupyter notebooks
s27.summary: This is an explanatory article about the Jupyter project and its notebook ecosystem for scientific computing and data analysis. It discusses architectural decisions including language-independent client–kernel separation, JSON-based sharable documents, format conversion, customizable interfaces, kernel wrappers and extensions, and support for reproducible and interactive experimentation.

s28.title: 5 reasons why jupyter notebooks suck
s28.summary: This is an opinion article about using Jupyter notebooks in collaborative data-science and machine-learning projects. It discusses limitations in version control, IDE and linting integration, testing, reproducibility from non-linear execution, and long-running asynchronous workloads, recommending separate Python projects for production pipelines while retaining notebooks for exploration.

s29.title: Jupyter Notebook is the Cancer of ML Engineering
s29.summary: This technical commentary examines Jupyter Notebook as a development environment for data science and machine-learning projects. It discusses integrating exploratory notebook code into production pipelines, including decisions about caching and execution state, dependency isolation, reproducibility, code reuse, orchestration, testing, and using IDEs with notebook support.
